newsitem.title: UK: UK Chancellor says delay likely in Euro timetable.
newsitem.headline: UK Chancellor says delay likely in Euro timetable.

text.p: The introduction of a single European currency, scheduled to start in 1999, is likely to be delayed, British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said in a BBC television interview.
When asked if delay was inevitable Clarke replied "Not inevitable but it's likely in my view."
In Germany, rising unemployment could drive up the fiscal deficit making it impossible for the government to meet the convergence criteria required for EC members to join a single currency, he said.

When asked about the recent strength of the pound on foreign exchange markets and whether it was damaging industrial exports, Clarke said it would be damaging to cut interest rates in an effort to reduce its strength.

"In the late 80s it was going up to three deutschmarks. Our governmnent then reduced interest rates to try to weaken the pound against the deutchmark. It was one of the things that caused hyper-inflation. We are not going to make that mistake again."

The pound has gained some 15 percent in the last six months. The official bank base rate, currently 6.0 percent, was last raised by 0.25 percentage points in October 1996. Economists expect the next move to be upward given the prevailing strength of economic activity.

The government has a medium target of 2.5 percent for the underlying rate of inflation. The central bank's inflation report, released earlier this month, called for a moderate rate rise if that target was to be met.
